canDo: Can hold your position in a 4–5-minute debate against the examiner’s repeated objections: concede before rebutting, use hypotheticals to work through consequences, and adjust your view tactfully when necessary.
review: Review day 7’s contrast and concession (bien que, même si, avoir beau, certes… mais, il n’empêche que) and day 9’s hypothesis and condition (si + imperfect/conditional, à condition que, à moins que… ne, au cas où); build on the outline structure of day 36’s monologue.
input: Read: an analysis of “the flying dilemma”, a column arguing “travel less, travel better” and a letter from a reader in Réunion; mark every concessive structure and the real argument that follows it. Listen: a radio debate on taxing air tickets (twice), an interview with the mayor of a mountain town and a vox pop in Brussels; note each speaker’s concessions and rebuttals.
output: Write: a formal letter on behalf of a users’ association to the president of the regional council, asking for night trains to be brought back (≥250 words); you must anticipate and answer objections. Speak: a 6-minute monologue on a document about “individual flight quotas”, then a 4–5-minute debate with the examiner on “banning advertising for cheap flights”.
checkpoint: Reading and listening accuracy ≥80%; in the debate, use a different strategy (concede, refine, rebut, reaffirm) for each of 4 objections, with at least 3 concessive structures and 2 si hypotheticals, without repeating your opening statement word for word.
challenge: Today’s challenge: find a news item about transport and climate (trains, planes, air ticket taxes, etc.) on TV5MONDE or RFI’s « Journal en français facile » and record a 90-second response: first acknowledge an opposing view with « Certes… mais… », then work through a consequence with « Si l’on… , on… ».

questions.why: The article moves from “more and more people feel guilty” (paragraph 1) to “acting on it is still hard” (paragraph 3: « le passage à l’acte reste difficile »); the core is the gap between awareness and behaviour. A isn’t covered; C: the text actually says plane tickets are sometimes cheaper than the train.

bien que introduces a concession: the data are only what respondents “say”, which may not reflect real behaviour, so they must be read with caution. B is the opposite of « simples déclarations »; C: no one in the text questions the data.

« un seul aller-retour entre l’Europe et l’Amérique du Nord peut équivaloir à plusieurs mois de trajets quotidiens en voiture ». A contradicts « ne représente qu’une part limitée des émissions mondiales »; B: the text makes no such comparison.
The quote is a hypothetical: if there were more night trains, many people would “make the leap” to rail. A takes it literally; C goes too far: switching to the train doesn’t mean not travelling.

It first grants that « le changement est possible », then qualifies it with « Il n’empêche que la portée de cette décision reste limitée : seules quelques lignes sont concernées ». B (“unfair”) has no basis; C contradicts « limitée ».

« À moins que les pouvoirs publics ne rendent le train réellement compétitif, on ne changera pas les comportements à grande échelle ». A is the opposite of her doubts about « bonne volonté »; B isn’t argued in the text.

The title and the last paragraph, « remplacer la quantité par la qualité », sum up the text. A: the author clearly says « Je ne demande à personne de rester chez soi »; B: he actually criticises resort-style travel.
« On m’objectera que… Certes. Mais… »: the classic “concession + rebuttal” structure. A: he grants the other side’s point (« Certes »); C: he doesn’t give up his position.

« ils se nourrissent mutuellement », illustrated with a hypothetical: « si la demande de trains de nuit augmentait, les opérateurs finiraient par en proposer davantage ». B is the view he partly concedes and then rebuts.

« Ce n’est pas le voyage que je remets en cause, c’est sa transformation en produit de consommation rapide » (a cleft sentence). B is what he recommends; C: he thinks only slow, in-depth travel lets you really get to know local people.

« Je ne demande à personne… Je propose simplement… »: a gentle tone offering a constructive proposal. There is no threat (A) and no pessimism (C); on the contrary, he thinks it can help us “rediscover the joy of travel”.
« permettez-moi de rappeler une réalité souvent oubliée »: as an overseas resident, she adds an overlooked perspective. Neither B nor C is raised in the letter.

The aside between dashes, « je n’ai pas de voiture et je fais attention à ma consommation », proves she is « sensible aux questions climatiques », making her concession more credible. A is the opposite; C has no basis.
« je n’y verrais aucun inconvénient, à condition que les liaisons avec l’outre-mer soient traitées à part ». A and B contradict “no objection”.
If overseas routes aren’t treated separately, the cost will once again fall on overseas residents who have no alternative. B and C misread what « les mêmes » refers to.
The host opens with: « faut-il taxer beaucoup plus lourdement les billets d’avion ? ». A is the opposite: night trains are the alternative both sides support; C is proposed by no one.

« le prix d’un billet ne reflète pas du tout le coût réel du vol pour l’environnement ». B isn’t mentioned; C: she mentions fuel tax on cars only as a comparison, not because she thinks it’s too high.
« Ceux qui ont les moyens continueraient de voler… tandis que les familles modestes… renonceraient ». He mentions neither A nor C.

« Je reconnais que le risque existe. C’est pourquoi nous proposons une taxe progressive »: she concedes, then adjusts the proposal. A contradicts her concession; B: she refines the idea rather than abandoning it.
« comment la contrôler ? … un registre de tous les vols » and « pousserait les voyageurs à partir des aéroports voisins ». Neither B nor C is mentioned.
Delaunay: « Là-dessus, nous pouvons nous rejoindre : si le train était plus rapide et moins cher… ». A is the opposite of a progressive tax; C: neither of them argues this.
The host introduces it: « fermer ses remontées mécaniques ». A: the mayor says that even with snow cannons it was losing money; B is the opposite of closing.
« Si nous avions continué, la commune se serait endettée pour des décennies » (a past hypothetical). B is the opposite: ski workers were angry; C isn’t mentioned.
« Je comprends leur colère, même si je reste convaincue que nous n’avions pas le choix »: understanding, but standing firm. A and C don’t match the recording.
« Bien que la fréquentation hivernale ait baissé, l’été attire désormais deux fois plus de monde ». B contradicts this; C: most of them retrained as mountain guides.
être au pied du mur is an idiom meaning “to have your back to the wall, to have no choice”. She advises changing course early, while there are still resources. A and C are literal misreadings.
« ils ont adoré dormir dans le train. Pour nous, ça fait partie du voyage ». A contradicts the children “loving it”; B: she doesn’t mention price.
« j’ai deux semaines de congé par an. Si je passe deux jours dans les transports, il ne me reste presque rien ». A contradicts « Bien que je sois conscient du problème »; C isn’t mentioned.
« Ça dépend de la destination »: the train for short trips, but the plane for a long trip to Canada. B and C both contradict « je n’hésiterais pas une seconde à prendre l’avion ».

V37-01.zh: a matter of conscience, a moral dilemma
V37-01.exZh: For many families, booking a long-haul flight has become a matter of conscience.

V37-02.exZh: We can’t rely on travellers’ goodwill alone to cut emissions.

V37-03.exZh: No need for long speeches: the figures speak for themselves.

V37-04.zh: to have limited reach, limited impact
V37-04.exZh: The law has limited impact, as it only covers three routes.

V37-05.exZh: Without competitive trains, behaviour can’t be changed on a large scale.

V37-06.exZh: The figures are telling: a short-haul flight emits far more than a train journey.

V37-07.zh: to point the finger at someone (often in the negative)
V37-07.exZh: I’m not pointing the finger at anyone: I’ve made the same mistakes.

V37-08.zh: to reinforce each other, to go hand in hand
V37-08.exZh: Individual choices and public policy go hand in hand.

V37-09.exZh: A hike close to home can hold unexpected surprises.

V37-10.zh: a change of scene, a sense of being somewhere else
V37-10.exZh: You don’t have to go to the ends of the earth for a change of scene.

V37-11.exZh: Travelling less often can restore the flavour of travel.

V37-12.exZh: For families in overseas departments, flying isn’t a whim but a necessity.

V37-13.exZh: If you’d rather meet online, I have no objection.

V37-14.exZh: Routes to overseas territories should be treated separately.

V37-15.exZh: If tickets were more expensive, people would think twice before leaving.

V37-16.exZh: With a progressive tax, the first flight of the year would be taxed very lightly.

V37-17.exZh: If the tax were too heavy, travel would once again become a privilege of the rich.

V37-18.zh: to agree (on a point), to find common ground
V37-18.exZh: Despite their differences, the two guests eventually found common ground on trains.

V37-19.exZh: This argument supports a decision at European level, not inaction.

V37-20.exZh: We didn’t close the ski slopes willingly.

V37-21.zh: to have one’s back to the wall, to have no choice
V37-21.exZh: Rather than waiting until your back is to the wall, prepare to change course early.

V37-22.exZh: For ten years, the resort has had only six weeks of snow cover.

V37-23.zh: on a trial basis, as a pilot
V37-23.exZh: We propose reopening the line on a trial basis in summer.

V37-24.exZh: The question of flight quotas has entered public debate.

V37-25.exZh: New planes are less fuel-hungry than old ones.

title: Speaking II: the debate
